body_markdown:
> *A look at how Tapestry is developing the next generation of craftspeople and creative talent.*


Roughly a decade ago, we recognized an opportunity: we could help early design professionals turn their potential into fully realized skill and experience.


So, we created the Tapestry Apprenticeship Program.


Aaron Rivera, Junior Patternmaker and former apprentice.


Today, the apprenticeship is a year-long, full-time contract role that gives roughly 20 recent graduates and early-career professionals hands-on design experience across the Coach and Kate Spade New York brands.


The program is for anyone who wishes to launch a career in fashion, and all that’s required to apply are a strong portfolio and creative streak. No degree required – just a passion for craftsmanship.


Apprentices apply to a specialty such as ready-to-wear, footwear, 3D design, leather goods, or concept design. Throughout the year, they work alongside designers and creatives from Coach and Kate Spade at either our New York headquarters in Hudson Yards or our North Bergen facility in New Jersey.


*Aaron Rivera, Junior Patternmaker and former apprentice.*


“The program isn’t designed to be a one year stop on someone’s resume,” said Diane Lwaysi, an Associate on Tapestry’s Talent Acquisition team. “It’s really here for us to grow the next generation of talent and hopefully give them a career here.”


An apprentice working on Tapestry’s in-house edge-stain process.


*An apprentice working on Tapestry’s in-house edge-stain process.*


So, you get accepted. What does the year look like?


The first week is a crash course on how to be a Coach or Kate Spade designer 101. Apprentices aretaught the industry calendar, meeting cadence, company culture, and meet the cross-functional partners they’ll work with.


Working sessions are also a massive part of the year, where apprentices meet and hear from leaders across our brands. These include industry presentations to store visits guided by retail associates to see first-hand who they’re designing for and why.


“They come to these sessions and they’re all absorbing the most information they can,” said Lwaysi. “I always see those apprentices shine and their teams come back to me saying, ‘we want to bring them on full time.’”


All this culminative knowledge builds to the pinnacle of the program: the spring presentation, where each apprentice independently creates and presents a product or idea to the brand design leaders. Apprentices get free creative reign and can present anything from a full ready-to-wear collection to a shoelace or button prototype.


A craftsperson at work in our Hudson Yards workshop.


*A craftsperson at work in our Hudson Yards workshop.*


The experience mirrors a professional design review: apprentices present their idea, connect it to the Coach or Kate Spade brand, and make a case for the concept to stakeholders.


“The way that these apprentices show up is so impressive,” said Lwaysi. “How professional they are. How well put together their presentations are. It’s incredible.”


The final presentation, and the entire year, are critical learning moments where apprentices build foundational skills and learn invaluable industry information. It’s more than a foot in the door; it’s true industry immersion and access to career building experiences.


Interested? Applications for next year are live until January 25, 2027: https://lnkd.in/gRXuZkjd
